summary: The driver is postgres.js 4.1.1; it documents certificate-always-checked and no channel binding, not 'TLS options ignored'. On workerd both are platform limits, and every TLS option except expectedServerHostname is ignored.
live: The competing driver is postgres.js (npm `postgres` 4.1.1, README section on Cloudflare Workers, first present in v4.0.0). It states the certificate is always checked, that channel binding is unavailable because Workers sockets do not expose the certificate, and that `sslnegotiation: 'direct'` is refused because sockets cannot send ALPN; it never says TLS options are ignored. Measured on the pinned workerd: the platform itself does all three. A self-signed untrusted, a wrong-name and an expired certificate were each rejected 5/5 and the server logged no authenticated session (cert.verification). `rejectUnauthorized:false`, `ca`, `servername`, `alpn`/`alpnProtocols` and a client certificate with key were ignored 0/5 on both connect() and startTls() (the Bun control honoured every one 5/5, so the probes can see an honoured option). `startTls({expectedServerHostname})` is the one TLS option that works: a wrong name is rejected, the right name fixes a connect-by-IP, and it becomes the SNI value, 5/5 each. No member of Socket, SocketInfo or the cloudflare:sockets module exposes the peer certificate or a hash (p2.surface 5/5), so tls-server-end-point and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS cannot be computed. Direct TLS to PostgreSQL 17 and 19.0 failed 0/5: the ClientHello has no ALPN and the server logged 'direct SSL connection request without ALPN'. So the driver's statements are platform limits on workerd; whether Cloudflare's production runtime has the same limits was not observed.
corrected: postgres.js 4.1.1 documents that on Workers the server certificate is always checked and that `channel_binding: 'require'` is rejected because the sockets do not expose the certificate. On workerd 1.20261118.1 both are platform limits: connect() and startTls() ignore rejectUnauthorized, ca, servername, alpn and client-certificate options, startTls() honours only expectedServerHostname, no API exposes the peer certificate, and a direct-TLS ClientHello carries no ALPN. Not verified on Cloudflare production.

summary: No socket at global scope: confirmed. TLS options and channel binding constrained: confirmed. Connection-count limits: not seen locally (50 sockets, none queued); the 6 is documented-only.
live: Global scope: connect() at module evaluation threw in 5 of 5 fresh workerd processes with the message 'Disallowed operation called within global scope' (p4.global-scope). TLS options and channel binding: see R-01 (ignored options, no certificate API, no ALPN). Connection count: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 24 and 50 sockets from one invocation all logged in, all were seen at once by pg_stat_activity, all ran pg_sleep(1) in parallel (about 1 s wall), and the proxy saw every TCP connection arrive within a few milliseconds, so nothing was queued, on PostgreSQL 17 (5/5 each) and for N = 8 and 50 on 19.0. Six idle sockets did not stop a seventh from opening. The embedder (workerd) sets no such limit; Cloudflare's documented limit of six was not observed.
corrected: Workers sockets cannot be created at global scope (the call throws in every fresh isolate observed), TLS options other than startTls expectedServerHostname are ignored and no channel binding is possible (workerd, local). A connection-count limit was not observed locally and is documented as six connections waiting for response headers; production behaviour is Not verified here.

summary: Both address forms open a socket and `opened` yields SocketInfo.
live: connect({hostname, port}, options) was used in every probe. connect("127.0.0.1:port") with no options opened and reported secureTransport 'off' and opened-info keys remoteAddress and localAddress. The address in the string form was a loopback test server, not a production host.

summary: All three secureTransport modes behave as stated and the default is off.
live: 'starttls': p1.starttls (5/5). 'on': TLS from the first byte, proven by the ClientHello at the proxy and the server's direct-TLS log line (p1.direct-tls; the handshake then fails for lack of ALPN). 'off' is used by the concurrency, write and cancel probes (plaintext, 5/5), and a connect() with no options reported secureTransport 'off' (blocked.json).

summary: A startTls option exists that the docs do not list: expectedServerHostname is honoured. Every other TLS option tried is ignored.
live: The page lists only secureTransport and allowHalfOpen. On workerd startTls({expectedServerHostname}) works as described in R-01 (wrong name rejected 5/5, fixes a connect-by-IP 5/5, becomes the SNI 5/5). rejectUnauthorized, ca, servername, alpn, alpnProtocols, cert and key were accepted without error and had no effect, on connect() and on startTls() (0/5 each; the Bun control honoured them, 5/5). The pg-cloudflare source imports a TlsOptions type for startTls, which agrees with the option existing.
corrected: The documented SocketOptions are secureTransport and allowHalfOpen. startTls() also takes expectedServerHostname, which workerd honours (it verifies the certificate against that name and sends it as SNI); other TLS options passed to connect() or startTls() are silently ignored. Cloudflare production was not tested.

summary: startTls() throws on sockets not created with secureTransport 'starttls'.
live: On a socket created with 'off' it threw a TypeError ('The `secureTransport` socket option must be set to 'starttls' for startTls to be used.'); on 'on' it threw 'Cannot startTls on a TLS socket.' (5/5 each).

summary: startTls() returns a new socket and a second call is refused (TypeError); the locks must be released first or the new socket is unusable. The old socket's state is in the evidence file.
live: startTls() returned a usable new socket in p1.starttls (5/5). A second startTls() on the upgraded socket threw 'Cannot startTls on a TLS socket.' and the connection stayed usable (5/5). The page does not say that the original socket's reader and writer must be released before the call: with a lock held, or with a read outstanding (releaseLock throws 'Cannot call releaseLock() on a reader with outstanding read promises.'), startTls() itself does not throw but the returned socket's streams fail at first use ('The ReadableStream has been locked to a reader' / 'This WritableStream is currently locked to a writer'), 0/5 each, on PostgreSQL and on MySQL and MariaDB. reader.cancel() on the outstanding read, then releaseLock, then startTls() worked 5/5 on all three. In the first-run trace of p2.surface, after the call the original socket object still reported secureTransport 'starttls' and upgraded false, was not locked (the locks had been released), and its `closed` promise had already resolved (oldSocket in p2.surface); the new socket reported secureTransport 'on' and upgraded false as well, so the `upgraded` flag did not tell the two apart.
corrected: startTls() returns a new socket and may be called once; before calling it the caller must release the reader and writer locks, and an outstanding read() must first be settled with reader.cancel(), otherwise startTls() returns a socket whose streams are unusable. (workerd, local.)

summary: allowHalfOpen was passed as false in every probe and never varied; no half-close behaviour was tested.
live: Every probe created sockets with allowHalfOpen false. No probe made the server close its side while the client kept writing, so the stated default and the true-setting behaviour were not observed.

summary: `opened` resolves with remoteAddress (string) and localAddress (undefined) locally; the original socket's `closed` resolves after startTls(); a rejecting `closed` was not observed.
live: opened-info on a connected socket had remoteAddress of type string and localAddress of type undefined, on both the starttls socket and the upgraded one, matching 'may not always be set'. The `closed` promise of the original socket resolved as soon as startTls() had returned (oldSocket.closed in the first-run trace of p2.surface; the later runs kept only their checks). No probe observed `closed` rejecting, and `closed` for a socket the server closed was not observed.

summary: The writable accepted strings, ArrayBuffers, DataViews and a Uint16Array as well as Uint8Array; only a number was rejected.
live: Fresh socket per chunk type, bytes counted at the proxy: string 3 bytes (UTF-8), ArrayBuffer 8, Uint8Array 8, Uint8Array subarray 8, DataView 8, Uint16Array 8, number rejected with 'This TransformStream is being used as a byte stream, but received an object of non-ArrayBuffer/ArrayBufferView type'. So locally the writable is more permissive than the page says.
corrected: The socket's WritableStream accepts any ArrayBuffer or ArrayBuffer view, and a string (written as UTF-8), and rejects other values (workerd, local). The study's clients write Uint8Array only.

summary: No Cloudflare-owned address was reachable or testable from here.
live: The sandbox has no route to Cloudflare addresses, so a refusal of 1.1.1.1:53 in blocked.json says nothing about the platform rule: workerd answered every disallowed or unreachable address with the same text. The production rule is documented-only.

summary: connect() at global scope throws 'Disallowed operation called within global scope'.
live: Module evaluation of the probe Worker called connect(); in 5 of 5 fresh workerd processes it threw an Error whose message begins 'Disallowed operation called within global scope. Asynchronous I/O (ex: fetch() or connect()), setting a timeout, and generating random values are not allowed within global scope.' The postgres.js statement that a connection belongs to the request that opened it is covered by D-15.

summary: No limit on open sockets was seen locally (50 open at once); production counting is documented-only.
live: 50 sockets from one invocation were all open and used at once (5/5), so the stated maximum of simultaneously open connections is not enforced by this workerd. Whether Cloudflare counts every open socket toward its limit was not observed. D-14 records the limits page's narrower wording.

summary: Port 25 could not be distinguished from a closed port here.
live: connect() to 127.0.0.1:25 was refused with the generic 'proxy request failed, cannot connect to the specified address', as was every other refused address; nothing listens on port 25, so a port-25 rule cannot be told from a refusal by the host. The message 'Connections to port 25 are prohibited' was not seen.

summary: With an outbound service that does not allow local addresses, loopback and localhost are refused with the quoted message; production blocking is documented-only.
live: workerd with outbound allow ["public"]: 127.0.0.1 and `localhost` both failed with 'proxy request failed, cannot connect to the specified address'. With ["public","local"] both opened, and an unrouted private address (10.255.255.1) was still refused with the same text. The rule here is the embedder's, not Cloudflare's; the page's claim about production is unverified.

summary: No queueing at 7, 8, 24 or 50 sockets locally; the documented limit counts connections waiting for response headers, and no production run exists.
live: Local workerd: N = 7, 8, 24 and 50 all logged in and were usable at once, opened within a few milliseconds of each other at the proxy (not queued); a cancel socket opened immediately as the 8th while 6 other sockets were busy. The limits page counts connections 'waiting for response headers' and the sockets page counts open sockets (D-11); the two readings were not separated because the limit does not exist locally. Run the production probes (runbook) to separate them.

summary: A socket created in one request fails in another with the quoted message.
live: A socket created and logged in during one HTTP request was used from a second request to the same isolate: the query and the write both failed with 'Cannot perform I/O on behalf of a different request. I/O objects (such as streams, request/response bodies, and others) created in the context of one request handler cannot be accessed from a different request's handler.' (I/O type: Writable), 5/5. The Bun control, which has no request boundary, used the socket 5/5.

summary: The certificate is always verified, whatever options are passed.
live: Untrusted self-signed, wrong name and expired were each rejected 5/5 with no session reaching PostgreSQL (server log: certificate unknown, bad certificate, certificate expired). rejectUnauthorized:false changed nothing (0/5). Trust here is the test CA given to workerd; 'publicly trusted CA' was not tested.

summary: Sockets expose no server certificate, so no channel binding is possible.
live: The full surface of Socket, its readable and writable, the opened-info and the module exports was listed before and after the upgrade: socket members are close, closed, opened, readable, secureTransport, startTls, upgraded, writable; the module exports connect and an internal helper. None of the 10 names a driver would look for (peerCertificate, getPeerCertificate, getCertificate, certificate, cert, tlsInfo, getProtocol, getCipher, tlsSocket, alpnProtocol) exists, 5/5 runs; the only TLS-related members report state (secureTransport, upgraded), not the certificate. The server offered SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS in every TLS session; the Worker has no certificate hash to bind to.

summary: Direct TLS fails because the ClientHello has no ALPN, and an alpn option does not add one.
live: secureTransport 'on' to PostgreSQL 17 and 19.0 failed 0/5; the proxy parsed the ClientHello (no ALPN extension) and the server logged 'received direct SSL connection request without ALPN protocol negotiation extension'. connect({alpn:['postgresql']}) and the alpnProtocols spelling changed nothing (0/5); the Bun control with the same option succeeded 5/5.

summary: A failed TLS handshake surfaces as an opaque error whose text does not say why; the cause is only visible server-side.
live: For the self-signed, wrong-name and expired cases the Worker saw the same text, 'internal error; reference = <id>', while the server log showed three different alerts (certificate unknown, bad certificate, certificate expired). The driver's TLS_HANDSHAKE_FAILED code and its advice about publicly trusted CAs are consistent with that; a driver cannot tell the causes apart from the exception.
